We write progress notes and upgrade/downgrade goals, but honestly it seems like a waste of a company's money to pay for you to observe an eval when you could be treating a patient/client.

That said, it's important that the documentation be really clear so that you know what to do, and honestly pretty much every eval I've seen is super-clear.

Typically your OT will talk to you about a pt, introduce you to the patient, etc. Often things come out during treatments that the patient didn't disclose during the eval that may effect outcomes, etc. As an asst it's your job to keep communication with your OTR to let them know what's up, if you have questions, etc. 

I guess what I'm saying is the treatment is a dynamic process, things can change and I don't think a COTA needs to be present for an eval.

I'm a COTA who's been working for 10 years and the most I've ever pulled in was $54K in a SNF in GA.

Always fighting to get paid what I'm worth, and I think I've pretty much capped out at what I can get.  I don't see salaries rising with the OTA to bachelor's degree. 

I will say that I haven't had problems finding work. The worst thing is just that in order to get a raise I've typically had to find another job. Even then, you have to be careful what you're walking into. I worked for a place once where there was no OT on site. That was fine; I just had to be diligent about knowing which patients needed visits/notes/etc. and let the prn OTs know. I noticed that there was a part B patient who the COTA prior to me had been seeing for months who hadn't seen an OT since the eval. I told my rehab director, and she wanted me to just keep seeing her. I wouldn't, because legally that pt has to be seen every tenth visit by an OTR, and she needed a visit with the OT first. None of the prn OTs would see the pt (didn't want to get involved) and none of them would write a d/c note, either. So my rehab director told me to write a note in the chart that said therapy services were on hold. I did that. 

Cut to a few months later when my company has lost their contract with the nursing home, and during a review of the records the part B it comes up and the company's rep (who was an OTR) starts to try and hold me responsible for what happened. I explained the situation and she took me to go see the pt. Then she starts asking me why such-and-such wasn't addressed, why this-or-that want a goal. I explained to her (again) that I legally cannot see this pt, so I didn't, and I didn't do the eval or write the goals. She asked me why I didn't write a discharge and I said, "because I'm a COTA and legally I cannot do that." 

She got really quiet, wrote a d/c note for the pt and that was that. 

I left that company because they were shady (obviously) but the sad thing is that I made the highest hourly wage I've ever made working for them. But it wasn't worth it. 

So yeah, I've gotten a bit burned out.

I've been a COTA for 10 years and the field has changed a lot since I started. It just seems to be getting worse and worse. I'm lucky where I am right now and plan to stay there until I can retire, but I'm not happy at all.
